content: Want to stay on top of the science and politics driving biotech today? Sign up to get our biotech newsletter in your inbox. Good morning. Hope you all have a great Thanksgiving tomorrow! title: Despite stalling in court, Trump restrictions on foreign students have had a chilling effect on enrollment
summary: New data show a clear drop in the enrollment of international graduate students, a key piece of the U.S. biomedical workforce.
content: Even as judges have blocked visa restrictions and other limits on foreign scholars and scientists, the Trump administration is winning outside court. New data show a clear drop in the enrollment of international graduate students, a key piece of the U.S. biomedical workforce. That paradox was on full display last week. On Nov. 16, a federal judge issued a final ruling blocking a proposed four-year cap on how long international students and postdoctoral researchers can remain in the country. The next day, a judge in a separate case issued a preliminary injunction preventing the administration from narrowing eligibility for a work authorization program widely used by foreign students. title: Why Medicare’s 2027 physician pay changes worry some specialists
summary: Cuts to Medicare physician payment rates for certain same-day services could impact some specialists more than others.
content: Podiatrist Heather McGuire always wanted to serve in a clinic in her hometown of Ventura, Calif. Fifteen years after she opened her practice, she is realizing her dream in the community that raised her, treating suburbanites and agricultural workers with diabetes on Medicare. But McGuire believes that dream may be ending. Read the rest…

title: Opinion: Washington and Beijing are building walls around biotechnology. That’s the wrong approach
summary: “Data show that the U.S.-China contest in biotechnology is not one race but several,” writes Michael S. Kinch.
content: For more than a decade, my colleagues and I at the Center for Research Innovation in Biotechnology have tracked every experimental medicine that enters human testing anywhere in the world. Last December, I wrote in STAT that China had reached parity with the United States in terms of the absolute number of new drugs introduced into clinical trials each year. Starting in 2018, the rate of U.S. contributions began to stagnate. Meanwhile, in 2013, Chinese organizations had introduced about 30 new experimental drugs. A decade later, the number topped 400. And there is no reason to expect the momentum in either country is changing. Over the past month, both governments have seemingly been moving to wall themselves off. On Oct. 16, Beijing proposed barring foreign acquisition of its companies’ proprietary cell and gene platforms. Within a week, the U.S. Department of the Treasury proposed restrictions that would bar Americans from taking equity stakes, forming joint ventures, or making limited-partner investments in Chinese biotech companies and their equipment suppliers. title: STAT+: We’re reading about BioNTech founders’ oncology startup, a long-acting GSK drug, and more
summary: The cofounders of BioNTech are in talks to raise about $1 billion for a new oncology company
content: Hello again from STAT’s London outpost, with reporter Andrew Joseph here for Mr. Pharmalot. This newsletter will be off tomorrow and Friday, and while Thanksgiving is a U.S. holiday, it never hurts to take a moment to feel some gratitude, wherever you might be. In the meantime, a few tidbits for your day. … The cofounders of BioNTech are in talks to raise about $1 billion for a new oncology company, as they prepare to step down from the Covid-19 vaccine maker , the Financial Times reports. Uğur Şahin and Özlem Türeci, the husband-and-wife team behind the German company, are speaking with potential investors about the funding round, which is being led by European venture capital firm Plural. Their new company will be called Arife and will focus on using messenger RNA to treat cancer. A long-acting drug from GSK performed at least as well as an existing treatment for patients with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, potentially setting up the medicine to be a less burdensome option for patients , Fierce Pharma shares. The non-inferiority study tested Exdensur, which was dosed just twice over a year, versus GSK’s other drug Nucala, which required monthly treatment. Exdensur resulted in remission rates at least on par with those from Nucala, and the drugs had similar adverse event rates. GSK says the results give it confidence that Exdensur now has a shot at becoming the first ultra-long-acting option for EGPA. Continue to STAT+ to read the full story…
